content:
Ray-Ban Meta Glasses and the latest cheaper non-designer option are sold on the basis of the built-in AI features, but in early July the company announced a “ridiculous” limit on the free usage you can make of an accessibility feature.

Effectively, Meta has retroactively applied a paywall to a hardware product it already sold to customers. Update: The social network has now said it is “pausing” plans to paywall the feature – see the end of the piece.

Meta first started rolling out the Conversation Focus feature in December of last year.

That’s a smart use of AI, and one of the best things about it is that it uses on-device processing, meaning that privacy isn’t compromised and mobile data isn’t needed.

However, The Verge reports that Meta is now applying a limit to how much you’re allowed to use the feature without paying extra for it.

This is doubly unacceptable. First, as the site’s Sean Hollister points out, because the feature works on the device, there is no use of Meta servers and therefore no possible justification for charging for it. Second, this is an accessibility feature, and some may have purchased the glasses specifically for that reason.

Top comment by KJ705

It's difficult to imagine the paywalling an accessibility function will play well over time.

Accessibility related: I recently got my mother a pair of Airpod Pro 3 earbuds specifically for the hearing aid functionality. I was VERY impressed with the hearing aid function, but I do wish it did better cancelling out background noise. She has found it very useful.

When asked for comment by The Verge, Meta said that the limit “currently” applies only to the Conversation Focus feature, implying that other AI features may be rate-limited in future. The company told us that it doesn’t consider it to be an accessibility feature given that it is intended for use by those with normal hearing. I would argue that this is semantics, as some struggle more than others to hear conversations in noisy environments.

All this may be good news for the upcoming Apple Glasses – it helps provide another reason for consumers to buy their AI-powered glasses from a more reputable company even though the upfront cost is likely to be higher. The company has always said that it never seeks a return on investment for accessibility features, rather viewing this as a way to contribute to a better world.

Apple Glasses are expected to launch at some point next year.

Update: Meta told The Verge that it has paused plans to limit access to Conversation Focus, but has not given up the idea of paywalling some features for the glasses.
